text: Creating a user@host account gives someone the ability to authenticate — it grants nothing else. A freshly created MySQL account can log in and do essentially nothing until privileges are explicitly granted.

MySQL privileges apply at exactly one of four levels: global with the star-dot-star syntax covering every database, database level covering every table in one database, table level naming one exact table, and column level restricting SELECT or UPDATE to specific columns only.

Privileges aren't just ALL or nothing. A DBA deliberately grants individual privileges like SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, ALTER, and EXECUTE. GRANT OPTION is a special one — it lets the grantee pass their own access on to other accounts, so it's handed out sparingly.

REVOKE mirrors GRANT's exact syntax and is the standard way to strip an account down before locking or deleting it. SHOW GRANTS FOR an account returns its current privileges as the exact GRANT statements that would reproduce them — the fastest way to audit access.
Grant the narrowest privilege at the narrowest scope the job actually requires. Next up: roles in MySQL 8, a newer way to group privileges instead of granting them one account at a time.
